name: Göreme Open-Air Museum
desc: Eleven rock-cut chapels and a monastic refectory packed into one hillside bowl, the whole thing carved out of soft tuff. The Dark Church still carries deep blue 11th-century frescoes because centuries of pigeon droppings sealed it from daylight. Tokalı Church, the largest and best painted, sits across the road on the same ticket.
season: Apr–May and Oct; January snow on the cones is worth the cold and the slippery stairs
tip: Do the Dark Church first at opening, then Tokalı across the road — most groups skip Tokalı entirely because it is outside the fence.
rev: Visitors rate the frescoes among the best Byzantine painting anywhere, but complain about the queue and no-photo rule in the Dark Church, the constant tour-group shuffle on narrow stairs, and a ticket price that has roughly doubled in three years.
entry: ≈€20 · Dark Church ≈€8 extra · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then shuttle to Göreme; the museum is a 15-minute uphill walk from the village

name: Rose Valley (Güllüdere)
desc: Pink and cream tuff folded into fins that go coral in the last hour of light. The 4 km path from Çavuşin passes apricot terraces, painted dovecotes and two rock churches — Haçlı, with a carved cross in its ceiling, and Üç Haçlı, where a caretaker unlocks the door for a coin.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; midsummer afternoons are shadeless and over 33 °C
tip: Start at Çavuşin and walk up rather than driving to the Kızılçukur sunset terrace, which fills with minibuses by 18:00.
rev: Walkers call this the best two hours in Cappadocia; the standard gripes are unsigned trail forks, informal fees collected at the churches, and dust from ATV tours cutting through the same gullies.
entry: Free — ≈₺100 (€2.50) collected informally at the rock churches
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Göreme; taxi or dolmuş to Çavuşin and walk back

name: Red Valley (Kızılçukur)
desc: The darker twin of Rose Valley, its iron-stained rock running from rust to violet as the sun drops. Narrow slots squeeze between walls barely shoulder-width, and the Üzümlü church hides grapevine frescoes above a vineyard. Locals still keep pigeon houses cut into the cliffs for fertiliser.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the clay path turns to slick paste after rain
tip: The two valleys interlock — take the marked link path near the vineyard and you can loop Red and Rose in one three-hour walk.
rev: Hikers love the colour and the emptiness at midday, then find the sunset viewpoint commercialised with a paid terrace, loud music and coach parties; the trail itself is unmarked in places and easy to lose.
entry: Free · terrace cafés charge ≈₺150 (€3.50) for the sunset spot
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Göreme or Ortahisar; the trailhead is a 20-minute walk from Ortahisar village

name: Love Valley
desc: A flat-bottomed corridor of the tallest, most improbably shaped fairy chimneys in Cappadocia, some over 30 metres with basalt caps. The floor is sandy and easy walking between vineyards; at dawn balloons drift right down the length of it. The name is a joke everyone gets immediately.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; snow in the valley in Jan–Feb photographs beautifully
tip: Walk in from the Göreme–Uçhisar road at the bottom instead of stopping at the paid roadside viewpoint — the chimneys only work from below.
todo: Walk the valley floor at dawn
Vineyard cave winery at the far end
rev: Universally photographed and genuinely striking, though people report the top viewpoint is now a fenced car park with an entry charge, quad bikes churn the sand, and there is no shade at all after 11:00.
entry: Free from the valley floor · roadside viewpoint car park ≈₺100 (€2.50)
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then Göreme; the lower entrance is 2 km on foot from the village along the Uçhisar road

name: Pigeon Valley
desc: The 4 km link between Göreme and Uçhisar, its cliffs drilled with thousands of hand-cut pigeon holes, many with painted red-ochre borders to guide the birds home. Farmers collected the droppings for the vineyards for centuries. The path ends climbing to Uçhisar castle with the whole plateau behind you.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov; parts flood briefly after spring storms
tip: Walk it uphill from Göreme to Uçhisar in the late afternoon and take the dolmuş back — the reverse leaves you climbing into the sun.
rev: An easy, shaded, genuinely quiet walk by Cappadocian standards; the complaints are the evil-eye tree viewpoint being a tour-bus scrum, litter near the Göreme end, and a couple of short scrambles that surprise people in the wrong shoes.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then Göreme; dolmuş from Uçhisar back to Göreme runs roughly hourly

name: Meskendir Valley
desc: A narrow green cut between Göreme and Ortahisar where the path runs under rock arches and through short unlit tunnels cut by farmers. Apricot and mulberry trees close overhead, dovecotes line the walls, and you can walk an hour on a weekday without meeting anyone.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the tunnels stay cool even in July
tip: Bring a torch for the two tunnels and link it with Kızılçukur at the top for a proper half-day loop back to Göreme.
rev: Repeatedly named the quietest of the Göreme valleys, with the caveat that the trail is badly signed where it crosses the campsite road and vanishes entirely in one overgrown stretch after rain.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then Göreme; the trailhead is by the campsite on the Ortahisar road

name: Zemi Valley
desc: The longest of the Göreme valleys, running southwest towards Uçhisar with a seasonal stream, poplars and no road access for most of its length. El Nazar Church stands alone in a cone near the entrance with 10th-century frescoes; the Sakli (Hidden) Church nearby was only found in 1957.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; stream crossings after snowmelt in March
tip: El Nazar has its own caretaker and closes early — call in on the way out of Göreme rather than at the end of the walk.
rev: People come out of Zemi saying it feels like Cappadocia before tourism, then note the churches are often locked, the path braids into dead ends among the orchards, and phone signal disappears halfway along.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Göreme; the valley starts below the Open-Air Museum road, 10 minutes on foot

name: Devrent Valley
desc: A small lunar bowl between Zelve and Avanos with no churches and nothing carved — just eroded pale rock that reads as camels, seals and hooded figures depending on where you stand. It takes twenty minutes to walk and works best in flat morning light when the shapes have edges.
season: Year-round; best in the first hour after sunrise
tip: The camel rock everyone photographs is on the right of the road, but the better ground is the unmarked path uphill on the left, where nobody goes.
todo: Upper path away from the car park
rev: Fine as a fifteen-minute stop and free, but frequently described as the weakest item on the standard Red Tour — coaches unload, everyone shoots the camel, and the souvenir stalls outnumber the formations.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then the Avanos–Ürgüp road; it is a roadside stop 5 km from Zelve

name: Uçhisar
desc: A single tuff outcrop riddled with rooms, tunnels and tombs, rising above a village of cave houses at the highest point in Cappadocia. From the top you see Erciyes, Hasan Dağı and every valley at once. The lanes below still have collapsed dwellings that people moved out of in the 1960s.
season: Year-round; the summit platform is exposed and brutal in a winter wind
tip: Climb at sunrise when the balloons launch below you rather than at sunset, when the small platform is standing-room only.
todo: Roman rock tombs on the north face
rev: The view is the best in the region by common consent; the recurring complaints are steep worn steps with poor railings, a genuine crush at sunset, and a village that has gone almost entirely over to boutique cave hotels.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport 10 km, or Kayseri (ASR) 70 km; dolmuş from Göreme takes 10 minutes

name: Ortahisar
desc: Uçhisar's overlooked sibling: an 86-metre rock citadel over a square where old men still play okey, and a warren of cold-storage caves that hold Turkey's lemons and potatoes through winter. Stone Ottoman houses and a small ethnography museum sit below. Far fewer hotels, and prices to match.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the citadel closes in high wind
tip: Ask at the square about the citrus storage caves — the refrigeration trade, not tourism, is what keeps this village going.
rev: Travellers who base here say it is the authentic version of Göreme with real village life; the trade-offs are fewer restaurants, an early-closing citadel with a rickety metal stair, and almost no evening transport.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 15 km by road; dolmuş from Ürgüp or Göreme every 30–60 minutes

name: Çavuşin
desc: Half-abandoned cliff village whose old rock houses were evacuated after a rockfall, leaving open rooms hanging above the new settlement. The Church of St John the Baptist, one of the oldest in Cappadocia, sits at the top of an iron stair; the Nicephorus Phocas church by the road has vivid 10th-century soldiers.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the stair to the basilica is dangerous when icy
tip: The Nicephorus Phocas church at the foot of the cliff is a separate ticket and takes ten minutes — most people drive past it to Paşabağ.
todo: Climb to St John the Baptist
Start the Rose Valley walk here
rev: Praised as the best trailhead in Cappadocia and pleasantly ruinous, but the collapsed village is genuinely unstable, the upper basilica is often roped off, and the coach car park below fills with carpet touts by mid-morning.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then the Göreme–Avanos road; dolmuş from Göreme takes 10 minutes

name: Zelve Open-Air Museum
desc: Three converging valleys of cave dwellings lived in until 1952, when erosion made them unsafe and the village moved down the road. You walk through kitchens with soot on the ceilings, a rock-cut mosque with its minbar, a mill, and the Üzümlü and Balıklı churches, all on the same terrain the residents used.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; no shade anywhere in the three valleys
tip: Take a torch and use the 30-metre unlit tunnel linking valleys one and two — most visitors turn back at the barrier and walk the long way round.
rev: Often called more atmospheric than Göreme because you can actually go inside the rooms; the frequent complaints are steep loose scrambles, several sections fenced off after rockfalls, and zero shade or water once you are in.
entry: ≈€10 · joint ticket with Paşabağ · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then the Avanos–Ürgüp road; a car or the Red Tour is the practical way in

name: Paşabağ (Monks Valley)
desc: The multi-headed fairy chimneys, some with two and three basalt caps on one stem, standing in an old vineyard. One cone is hollowed into a hermitage chapel for Simeon Stylites, reached by a steep internal stair with windows cut at the top where the hermit watched the valley.
season: Year-round; low winter sun gives the cones the strongest shadows
tip: Squeeze up the stair inside the St Simeon chimney — it is unmarked, easy to walk past, and the only chimney interior here you can enter.
rev: The most photogenic chimneys in Cappadocia and mercifully flat to walk, undercut by a large souvenir bazaar at the entrance, coach parties every fifteen minutes, and a ticket that now covers Zelve whether you want it or not.
entry: ≈€10 · joint ticket with Zelve · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then the Avanos road; 5 km from Avanos, usually visited on the Red Tour

name: Avanos
desc: The pottery town on the Kızılırmak, where the red clay from the riverbed has been thrown on kick-wheels since Hittite times. Workshops line the old streets below the Ottoman houses, and any of them will sit you at a wheel for half an hour. The river is the widest thing you will see in Cappadocia.
season: Apr–Oct for the river terraces; workshops are open all year
tip: Skip the coach-stop showrooms on the main road and walk up into the back lanes, where families still fire their own kilns and prices are a third of the ones on the tour circuit.
todo: Throw a pot on a kick-wheel
rev: Most people enjoy the wheel session and the riverside evening; the persistent complaints are hard-sell showrooms attached to tours, wildly inflated ceramic prices, and the hair museum in Chez Galip being either the highlight or deeply unpleasant, depending on the visitor.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport 18 km or Kayseri (ASR) 65 km; frequent dolmuş from Ürgüp and Göreme

name: Ürgüp
desc: The region's proper town rather than a tourist village: a working market, Greek and Ottoman stone houses on the Esbelli hill, and the Üç Güzeller chimneys on the edge of it. This is Cappadocia's wine country, and the old cellars around Temenni hill pour Kalecik Karası and Emir straight from the barrel.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the grape harvest and wine festival fall in September
tip: Saturday is the town market — go for the dried apricots and pekmez rather than the carpet shops on Kayseri Caddesi.
todo: Taste Emir white in a rock cellar
rev: Rated the most liveable base in Cappadocia with the best restaurants, though visitors note it is spread out, the sights are thin compared with Göreme, and hotel prices on Esbelli hill have climbed well past what the town otherwise costs.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 75 km or Nevşehir (NAV) 25 km; shuttles meet most flights and drop at the otogar

name: Mustafapaşa (Sinasos)
desc: The best-preserved Greek village in Cappadocia, emptied by the 1924 population exchange. Carved stone doorways with Greek inscriptions, the Ayios Vasilios and Constantine-Helena churches, and a main square that still looks like 1910. Students from the local faculty keep it from being a museum piece.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; very quiet and half-shut in midwinter
tip: Walk the 3 km down to the Gomeda valley behind the village — a rock-cut church, an old chapel and nobody else on the path.
todo: Carved Greek doorways on the lanes
rev: Visitors consistently call it the calmest place in the region and the stonework genuinely rare, while noting that several churches are locked with no visible keyholder, restoration has left scaffolding up for years, and there is little to do after dark.
entry: Village free · churches ≈₺100 (€2.50) each when open
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 6 km south of Ürgüp; dolmuş from Ürgüp runs about every hour

name: Derinkuyu Underground City
desc: Eighteen storeys cut into the tuff, eight of them open, going down 60 metres to a cruciform church and a 55-metre ventilation shaft that still draws cool air. Half-tonne millstone doors could be rolled shut from inside at each level. Thousands of people and their livestock sheltered here from raids.
season: Year-round; a constant 13 °C makes it the best stop on a 35 °C July day
tip: Go at opening or after 16:00 — mid-morning the single stooped staircase becomes two-way traffic and you queue underground, which is where claustrophobia usually starts.
rev: Staggering as an engineering feat, but the reports are consistent: long crouched passages, genuine bottlenecks when two groups meet, poor air in peak season, and a visit that lasts about 45 minutes for a rising ticket price.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport 30 km, then the Niğde road; dolmuş from Nevşehir otogar every 30 minutes

name: Kaymaklı Underground City
desc: Wider and lower than Derinkuyu, built around a central ventilation shaft with rooms fanning out from it — stables on the first level, a chapel, then kitchens with blackened ceilings and basalt blocks for grinding copper ore. Villagers above still use the top-level cellars for storage.
season: Year-round; steady 13 °C, welcome in July and August
tip: Follow the red arrows down and blue arrows up religiously — people who improvise end up crawling against the flow in a 1.2-metre-high tunnel.
rev: Generally described as easier and less claustrophobic than Derinkuyu with lower ceilings but shorter passages; complaints centre on tight two-way traffic at peak times, hawkers at the entrance, and guides rushing groups through in half an hour.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport 20 km on the Niğde road; frequent dolmuş from Nevşehir, 20 km short of Derinkuyu

name: Özkonak Underground City
desc: Found in 1972 by a farmer wondering where his irrigation water went, this one has a defensive trick the famous two lack: holes above the tunnels for pouring hot oil on anyone who forced a door. Four of ten levels are open, and on most days you will have them to yourself.
season: Year-round; cool inside, and the Avanos road is clear in winter
tip: There is no ticket queue and no tour schedule here — the caretaker walks you down and explains the oil holes, which no guide bothers with at Derinkuyu.
rev: Visitors who make the detour rate it the best-value underground city precisely because it is empty, while warning that the open section is small, lighting is patchy, and it is a 15 km dead-end drive north of Avanos with no public transport.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then Avanos and 15 km north on the Özkonak road; you need a car or a taxi

name: Hacı Bektaş Veli Complex
desc: The spiritual centre of Anatolian Alevism and Bektashi Sufism: three courtyards, a kitchen with the cauldron that fed dervishes, and the tomb of Hacı Bektaş Veli under a fluted dome. Pilgrims touch the threshold stone rather than step on it. The atmosphere is devotional, not archaeological.
season: Year-round; the August 16–18 commemoration fills the town completely
tip: Come outside the August festival if you want the tomb quiet, and note that visitors are expected not to tread on the marble threshold at the inner gate.
rev: Turkish visitors describe it as moving and quietly maintained; foreign visitors report almost no English signage, a museum layout that assumes you know the tradition, and a bleak 45 km drive across steppe to reach it.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 45 km northwest by road; buses from Nevşehir otogar run several times a day

name: Church of St Jean, Gülşehir
desc: A two-storey rock church whose upper chapel was cleaned of soot in 1995, revealing 1212-dated frescoes in reds and blues so fresh they look wrong — a Last Judgment, a whale swallowing Jonah, Christ on a ladder. It is the most vivid painted interior in Cappadocia and almost nobody stops here.
season: Year-round; the interior is dim on overcast days
tip: The lower level is unpainted and easy to mistake for the whole church — the stair to the frescoed upper chapel is around the outside to the right.
rev: Those who find it call the colour better than anything at Göreme and the solitude remarkable; the complaints are erratic opening hours, a caretaker who sometimes is not there, and no signage at all from the main road.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 20 km north on the Kırşehir road; dolmuş from Nevşehir, then a short walk

name: Cappadocia Hot-Air Ballooning
desc: Around a hundred balloons lift from the Göreme valleys before dawn, drifting low enough into Love and Rose valleys that the basket brushes the tuff, then climbing for the sunrise over the whole plateau. Flights last an hour, take off in the dark, and are strictly weather-dependent.
season: Flies year-round; Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct have the highest launch rate, winter the most cancellations
tip: Book for your first morning, not your last — roughly one in four winter mornings is grounded for wind and you want spare days to rerun it.
todo: Pre-dawn inflation on the launch field
Watch from a hotel terrace instead
rev: Almost everyone calls it worth the money once, then reports the same friction: 04:30 pickups, cancellations with slow refunds, crowded 24-person baskets on the cheap tickets, and prices that have roughly doubled since 2019.
entry: ≈€180–350 per person depending on basket size and season
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then Göreme; operators collect from every cave hotel in the dark

name: Nevşehir Castle
desc: A Seljuk fortress on the rock above the provincial capital, mostly walls and a keep, with the whole city and the Kaymaklı-scale underground complex of Kayaşehir beneath it — found in 2013 during a demolition and thought to be the largest in the region. The castle itself takes twenty minutes.
season: Year-round; the ramparts are windy and exposed all winter
tip: Combine it with the Kurşunlu Mosque complex and the Damat İbrahim Paşa library below — the castle alone does not justify the drive into Nevşehir.
rev: Locals use it as a viewpoint and it is free, but travellers report a heavily rebuilt structure with little original fabric, the Kayaşehir underground city still not properly open to visitors, and a city that most people only pass through.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport 25 km, or Kayseri (ASR) 100 km; all regional dolmuş routes pass the Nevşehir otogar

name: Ihlara Valley
desc: A 14 km canyon cut 100 metres into the plateau by the Melendiz river, green with poplars and willows where everything above is bare steppe. Around forty rock churches open off the walls — Yılanlı with its snake-punished sinners, Kokar with a hand of God on the ceiling. A staircase of 382 steps drops you in.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the canyon floor stays cool when the plateau is at 35 °C
tip: Start at Ihlara village and walk downstream to Belisırma, then arrange a taxi back — the standard tour drops everyone at the mid-valley stair and sees a third of it.
rev: Rated the best walk in Cappadocia for shade and water, with recurring complaints about the 382-step descent on the return, several churches locked or fenced, and the riverside restaurant platforms at Belisırma charging tourist prices for ordinary trout.
entry: ≈€10 for the valley · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 100 km southwest via Aksaray; buses run Aksaray–Ihlara, but a car is far easier

name: Selime Monastery
desc: The largest rock-cut complex in Cappadocia, at the north mouth of the Ihlara canyon: a basilica-sized cathedral hall with columns hewn from the rock, a kitchen with a soaring chimney, stables with feed troughs, and rooms opening onto sheer drops. The cone-topped village below is half cave, half stone.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the polished rock ramps are lethal when wet or icy
tip: Wear grippy shoes — the entry ramp is worn smooth and steep, and it is the single most common place people fall in Cappadocia.
rev: Frequently the surprise favourite of an Ihlara day and vast enough to lose people in, though visitors flag the slippery unprotected ramps, no railings above long drops, and tour groups given only twenty minutes for a site that deserves an hour.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then via Aksaray to the top of the Ihlara valley; part of every Green Tour

name: Güzelyurt (Gelveri)
desc: A Greek town of cut-stone houses stacked above the Manastır valley, where the 4th-century church of St Gregory of Nazianzus became a mosque in 1924 and kept its Byzantine bones. A monastery valley runs below with dozens of rock chapels, and the Sivişli church still has its frescoes.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; snow closes the higher lanes in January
tip: Ask at the Kilise Camii for the key to the Sivişli church down the valley — it is kept in the village and not advertised anywhere.
rev: Travellers rate it the most intact Greek-Cappadocian town after Sinasos and pleasantly untouristed, but note that half the churches need a key from someone who has gone to lunch and there are only a handful of places to eat.
entry: Village free · Kilise Camii and monastery valley ≈₺150 (€3.50)
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then via Aksaray; 12 km from Ihlara, best combined with it by car

name: Aşıklı Höyük
desc: A 10,000-year-old aceramic Neolithic mound on the Melendiz stream, older than Çatalhöyük, where people entered their mud-brick houses through the roof and buried their dead under the floors. Experimental reconstructions stand next to the excavation so you can see how the packed settlement actually worked.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; excavation season runs in summer, when you may see work in progress
tip: Go on a weekday in July or August and there is a decent chance an archaeologist on site will show you the trench and the roof-entry houses.
rev: Archaeology travellers find it genuinely important and free, while everyone else warns it is a low brown mound with minimal interpretation, no facilities, no shade, and a bumpy access track off the Ihlara road.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then the Aksaray–Ihlara road; 25 km southeast of Aksaray, car only

name: Ağzıkara Han
desc: A Seljuk caravanserai of 1231 on the old Konya–Kayseri road, with a carved portal, an open summer courtyard and a vaulted winter hall where camels and merchants slept in the same space. A small mosque stands on piers in the middle of the yard. Traffic on the modern highway roars past outside.
season: Year-round; the covered hall is cold and unheated in midwinter
tip: It sits right on the Aksaray–Nevşehir highway, so it costs you ten minutes on the drive between Cappadocia and Ihlara — most people never notice it.
rev: Visitors find it atmospheric and almost always empty, with the usual caveats: restoration has left some walls looking new, the caretaker's hours are informal, and there is nothing to do there beyond half an hour of looking.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) airport, then 15 km east of Aksaray directly on the D300 highway

name: Sultanhanı Caravanserai
desc: The biggest Seljuk caravanserai in Anatolia, built in 1229 and rebuilt after a fire, with a marble portal of interlocking geometry, a vast courtyard and a basilica-like stable hall lit only by a lantern dome. The scale is the point: it sheltered whole caravans crossing the salt plain.
season: Year-round; the courtyard bakes in July and the hall is icy in January
tip: Stand under the central dome of the covered hall and look up — the acoustics and the single shaft of light are what the photographs never get.
todo: Lantern dome in the stable hall
rev: Widely rated the best-preserved caravanserai in Turkey and worth the stop on the Konya road; complaints are heavy-handed restoration, a coach-tour rhythm in high season, and a plain highway town outside with little else in it.
onward: Konya (KYA) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport; 45 km west of Aksaray on the Konya highway, right in the village

name: Mount Hasan
desc: The 3,268-metre twin-peaked volcano that supplied the tuff all of Cappadocia is carved from, and possibly the mountain painted on a wall at Çatalhöyük 8,000 years ago. The walk from Karbeyaz plateau to the summit takes six hours through scree and old lava, with Tuz Gölü glinting to the north.
season: Jun–Sep for the summit; snow lies on the cone into May and returns in October
tip: Start from the Helvadere side before 05:00 — the ridge above 2,800 m is loose volcanic scree and the wind picks up hard by early afternoon.
rev: Climbers call it a straightforward but long scree slog with a huge view; the warnings are consistent — no water above the plateau, fast weather changes, an unmaintained upper path and a rough track to the trailhead.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Aksaray and 30 km south to Helvadere; a car is essential

name: Lake Tuz (Aksaray shore)
desc: Turkey's second-largest lake is barely a lake at all by August — a white salt pan you can walk out onto for a kilometre, water a few centimetres deep, turning pink from Dunaliella algae in high summer. Flamingos breed on the islands, and the Aksaray shore is the quieter side.
season: Jul–Sep for the pink water and salt harvest; in spring it is shallow brine and mud
tip: Walk out barefoot only if you have no cuts — the brine is savage — and rinse your shoes immediately, because dried salt destroys leather.
todo: Walk out on the salt crust
rev: Photographers love the pink water and mirror reflections; nearly everyone mentions the roadside stops on the Ankara highway are crowded and litter-strewn, the salt cuts feet, and outside July and August the lake can be simply grey mud.
entry: Free · some private shore access points charge ≈₺100 (€2.50) for parking
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Ankara (ESB) airport, then the Aksaray–Konya road; the quiet shore is near Eskil, car only

name: Nora (Viranşehir) and Helvadere
desc: The Hellenistic fortress where Eumenes of Cardia held out against Antigonus for a year in 320 BC, now a scatter of Byzantine chapels, cisterns and walls on a spur above Helvadere village. The trout restaurants by the reservoir below and the Hasan Dağı trailhead make it a good half-day.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the site is exposed and the track muddy after rain
tip: Ask in Helvadere for the Viranşehir track rather than trusting the map — the last kilometre is a farm road and the ruins are unsigned from the village.
todo: Byzantine chapel ruins on the spur
rev: Rewarding for people who like empty ruins and a view of Hasan Dağı; everyone else reports there is very little standing, no information boards, no ticket office and a rough approach that a low car will not enjoy.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Aksaray and 30 km south to Helvadere; car only

name: Gümüşler Monastery
desc: A rock-cut monastery around a courtyard sunk into the cliff, unknown until 1963 and therefore never vandalised. Its main church holds the only smiling Virgin in Byzantine art, still in original colour, plus a rare secular fresco of hunting scenes. There are grain pits, a crypt and a rock-cut tomb in the floor.
season: Year-round; interiors are dim, so go on a bright day and skip early morning
tip: Look up in the west chapel for the hunting fresco with a griffin — the caretaker will point out the smiling Virgin, but almost nobody is shown the secular painting.
rev: Consistently called the best-preserved frescoes in Cappadocia with a fraction of the visitors, though people note it is a plain suburb of Niğde, signage is thin, and the site takes only forty minutes once you have driven out here.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 130 km, or Adana (ADA); 10 km northeast of Niğde, dolmuş from the town centre

name: Aladağlar National Park
desc: Limestone walls and karst basins in the Anti-Taurus, with Demirkazık at 3,756 m and the Yedigöller plateau of seven small lakes at 3,000 m behind it. This is Turkey's best alpine rock, with big multi-pitch routes, ibex on the screes and shepherd camps in the high yaylas through summer.
season: Jun–Sep for the high routes; snow blocks the passes from November to May
tip: The Yedigöller crossing from Demirkazık to Kapuzbaşı is a serious two-day trek — hire a local guide in Çukurbağ, and do not attempt it without carrying water.
rev: Alpinists rate the limestone world-class and the solitude complete; the standard warnings are almost no marked trails or refuges, a bad-weather commitment far from help, and access roads that need a high-clearance vehicle.
entry: Free · guided trekking from ≈₺3,000 (€65) per day per group
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Adana (ADA) airport, then Niğde and 50 km east to Çamardı and Çukurbağ; car essential

name: Çamardı
desc: The base town under Demirkazık: a small grid of stone houses, a Thursday market where shepherds come down off the yayla, and a handful of trekking pensions that also run mule support into the Aladağlar. Apple orchards fill the valley, and the mountains stand up directly behind the last street.
season: Jun–Sep for trekking; deep snow and a very quiet town from December to March
tip: Book mules and a guide at the Çukurbağ pensions rather than from Niğde — the Çukurbağ families hold the actual permits and know the current state of the passes.
rev: Trekkers find the pensions warm and cheap and the logistics reliable; nobody pretends the town itself is scenic, and visitors mention limited food options, minibuses that stop by mid-afternoon, and almost everything shut out of season.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Adana (ADA) airport, then Niğde; dolmuş Niğde–Çamardı runs a few times daily, last one early afternoon

name: Narlıgöl Crater Lake
desc: A maar lake in a volcanic crater on the Melendiz range, green-blue and about 500 metres across, with hot springs bubbling up at the edge and a small thermal bath built over them. The rim road gives you the whole bowl at once; the water is sulphurous and warm where the springs enter.
season: Year-round; the thermal pools are best in Oct–Apr when the air is cold
tip: The spring water on the north shore runs at around 45 °C — go in the late afternoon on a winter day, when locals rather than tourists are in the pools.
todo: Soak in the hot spring pool
Drive on to the Ihlara plateau
rev: Visitors like the strangeness of a warm lake in bare steppe and the near-total absence of foreigners; the complaints are basic and rundown bath facilities, a strong sulphur smell, litter on the shore and an unsigned turn-off.
onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then the Niğde–Aksaray back road via Çiftlik; car only

name: Andaval (Church of Constantine and Helena)
desc: A 5th-century basilica standing roofless in a field at Aktaş, one of the oldest church buildings in Anatolia, with cut-stone apse walls and carved capitals still in place. The village around it is ordinary farmland; the Byzantine reliefs found here are now in the Niğde museum.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the field is muddy in spring and baking in July
tip: There is no ticket office and no fence — ask in Aktaş village for Andaval Kilisesi, because signage from the Niğde road is effectively nonexistent.
rev: Rewarding for anyone interested in early Christian architecture and completely free of visitors, but honestly a single ruined shell in a field, with no interpretation, no facilities and stones being carted off over the years.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Adana (ADA) airport, then Niğde; Aktaş is 10 km northeast of town, car or taxi

name: Tyana (Kemerhisar)
desc: The chief city of southern Cappadocia and home of Apollonius of Tyana, now a Roman aqueduct marching across a village at the edge of Kemerhisar, plus a spring-fed pool the Romans built and a mosaic-floored basilica under excavation. Locals still water fields from the same source.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; Bor plain summers are hot and shadeless
tip: The Roman pool by the spring is on the far side of the village from the aqueduct arches — most visitors photograph the arches and drive off without finding it.
rev: Ancient-history travellers enjoy piecing the city together, though reports agree it is thoroughly built over by the modern village, the excavation areas are fenced and often closed, and there is no visitor centre of any kind.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) or Adana (ADA) airport, then Niğde and 20 km southwest via Bor; dolmuş from Niğde to Kemerhisar

name: Mount Erciyes
desc: The 3,864-metre volcano that dominates every view in Kayseri and supplied the ash that became Cappadocia. Its northern flank carries Turkey's largest ski area — over 100 km of pisted runs and gondolas from Tekir Yaylası — and in summer the same lifts serve walkers heading for the crater rim.
season: Dec–Mar for skiing with reliable snow; Jul–Sep for the summit scramble
tip: Lifts run from Develi on the south side too, and that base is emptier and cheaper than Tekir on winter weekends when Kayseri comes up en masse.
todo: Night skiing on the Tekir pistes
rev: Skiers rate the snow reliable, the lifts modern and the prices a fraction of the Alps, then complain about wind holds closing the upper gondolas, weekend queues from the city, thin apres-ski and a summit route that is loose volcanic rubble.
entry: Ski day pass ≈₺1,600 (€35) · mountain access free in summer
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 25 km, then a 40-minute shuttle to Tekir Yaylası; ski buses run from Kayseri in winter

name: Sultan Marshes
desc: A Ramsar wetland where fresh and salt marsh meet on the Develi plain under Erciyes, with over 300 recorded bird species. Flamingos stand in the shallows through summer, cranes and pelicans pass in migration, and flat-bottomed boats push through reed channels from the Ovaçiftlik observation tower.
season: Apr–May and Sep–Oct for migration; flamingos stay into August
tip: Be at the Ovaçiftlik tower for first light and take the reed-boat trip then — by ten the heat haze makes long-lens work pointless.
todo: Flamingo flocks on the salt lake
rev: Birders rate it among Turkey's top wetlands and the boatmen knowledgeable, while noting water levels have dropped badly with irrigation, some years the salt lake is nearly dry, and facilities amount to one visitor centre and a tower.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 60 km south via Develi to Ovaçiftlik; a car is the only practical way

name: Kapuzbaşı Waterfalls
desc: Seven falls bursting straight out of a limestone cliff face 70 metres up, fed by underground karst rather than a river above — the water simply appears out of the rock. They sit at the bottom of the Aladağlar on the Zamantı river, and the spray keeps the gorge cold even in August.
season: May–Jul at full volume; by September the flow drops sharply
tip: The last 40 km from Yahyalı is a narrow gorge road with drops and no barrier — start early, and do not attempt it in the dark or in a wide vehicle.
rev: Those who make it call it the most spectacular waterfall in Anatolia and worth the whole day; every account also mentions the punishing access road, minimal facilities at the end and much less water after midsummer.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 130 km south to Yahyalı and a slow 40 km gorge road; high-clearance car recommended

name: Soğanlı Valley
desc: Two branching valleys with around a hundred rock churches, the best of them free-standing: Kubbeli, a domed chapel carved out of a single fairy chimney, and Karabaş with 11th-century frescoes on a black ground. Village women sell cloth dolls at the entrance, a Soğanlı craft going back generations.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the valley floor is muddy after rain and very quiet in winter
tip: Take the northern branch first for Kubbeli and Yılanlı, and pay the ticket at the entrance kiosk — the church doors up the valley are unlocked only if the warden knows you are in there.
todo: Kubbeli Church in a single cone
rev: Repeatedly described as Cappadocia thirty years ago, with the fair warnings that many frescoes are smoke-blackened or defaced, the churches are scattered over several kilometres of walking, and there is one restaurant and no public transport.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 90 km southwest via Yeşilhisar; from Ürgüp it is 60 km, car only

name: Talas
desc: The old Greek and Armenian hill quarter above Kayseri, where merchants who traded with Istanbul built black basalt mansions with carved doorways. Many are restored as cafés and boutique hotels now; the Panagia church and the Ali Dağı ridge above give the district its skyline, with Erciyes filling the horizon.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; pleasant evenings when central Kayseri is still hot
tip: Walk up to Ali Dağı at dusk for the city lights against Erciyes — paragliders use the same launch, and there is a tea kiosk at the top.
rev: Visitors like the stonework and the café scene and call it the pleasant side of Kayseri; the criticism is that restoration has been uneven, several landmark houses are closed or converted, and student nightlife makes the centre loud at weekends.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 15 km; city buses and the Kayseri tram reach Talas in 25 minutes from the centre

name: Kayseri Covered Bazaar and pastırma
desc: A 500-year-old bazaar wrapped around the black basalt citadel, with the Bedesten and Vezir Han still trading. The pastırma shops hang whole beef fillets crusted in çemen — fenugreek, garlic and paprika — cured since the Byzantine period, and the mantı here are thumbnail-sized and served under garlic yoghurt.
season: Year-round; pastırma is cured in autumn, so October has the fresh season's meat
tip: Buy pastırma cut from the sırt (loin) rather than the cheaper cuts, and ask for it sliced paper-thin in front of you — pre-packed vacuum trays are a different product.
todo: Pastırma and sucuk shops in the Bedesten
rev: Food travellers rate the pastırma the best in Turkey and the bazaar genuinely working rather than touristic; the complaints are a heavily modernised citadel interior full of chain shops, aggressive parking, and a city centre that is short on charm.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 5 km from the centre; the tram stops at the citadel and the bazaar is at its foot

name: Kültepe (Kanesh)
desc: The Assyrian merchant colony where over 23,000 cuneiform tablets were found — the oldest written records in Anatolia, private letters and contracts from around 1900 BC that name the earliest known Anatolian rulers. The mound and the lower karum town are excavated, with mud-brick house walls and street lines visible.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plain is exposed, with no shade on the excavation
tip: See the tablets and the Kültepe finds in the Kayseri Archaeological Museum first — the site itself is foundations, and it only makes sense once you have seen what came out of it.
rev: Historically one of the most important sites in Turkey, but visitors consistently report low mud-brick foundations, sparse signage, a site sometimes locked out of excavation season and very few other people — go for the story, not the spectacle.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 20 km northeast on the Sivas road towards Kültepe; car or taxi

name: Develi (Everek)
desc: A market town under the south face of Erciyes with a 13th-century Ulu Cami, the ruined Aziz Toros church from the Armenian quarter, and streets of cut-stone houses in the old Everek district. It is also the quiet approach to the Sultan Marshes and to Erciyes' southern ski lifts.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; winter is cold but the ski base is 20 minutes away
tip: The Everek quarter behind the main street is where the stone houses and the old church are — the modern centre gives no hint they exist.
rev: Worth an hour on the way to Sultansazlığı and pleasantly unvisited; the honest verdict is that the Armenian church is a roofless shell, much of the old quarter has been replaced by concrete, and there is little tourist infrastructure.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 40 km south by road; frequent buses from Kayseri otogar to Develi

name: Ağırnas
desc: Mimar Sinan was born here in 1490, and his family house — a stone building over a rock-cut cellar — is now a small museum. The real interest is underneath: a tunnel system linking cellars, wells and rooms across the village, dug into the same soft rock as the Cappadocian cities and still partly walkable.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; underground sections are cool and open year-round
tip: The underground passages are entered from the courtyard of the Sinan house — ask the attendant to unlock them, because they are not part of the standard walk-through.
rev: Architecture-minded visitors like the connection to Sinan and the odd underground layer; others find the museum thin, the tunnels only partly accessible, and the village largely rebuilt in modern concrete around the historic core.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport 20 km, then the Sivas road towards Ağırnas; city bus from Kayseri or a short taxi

name: Yahyalı and the Kapuzbaşı road
desc: Yahyalı weaves double-knotted wool carpets in madder red and indigo, still on looms in the villages, and it is where the road into the southern Aladağlar starts. Forty kilometres of single-track cut above the Zamantı gorge follow, past Kapuzbaşı, with cliffs on one side and a long drop on the other.
season: May–Oct for the gorge road; snow and rockfall close it in winter
tip: Fill the tank in Yahyalı — there is no fuel, no shop and barely any phone signal for the whole gorge stretch to Kapuzbaşı.
rev: Drivers describe the gorge as one of the great roads in Anatolia and the carpet workshops genuinely traditional; the same accounts warn of no barriers, blind bends, occasional rockfall and a carpet trade that has shrunk to a few families.
onward: Kayseri (ASR) airport, then 130 km south; buses reach Yahyalı, but the gorge road needs your own vehicle

name: Cacabey Madrasa
desc: A 1272 Seljuk madrasa built as an astronomical observatory, with a shaft in the courtyard floor used for star sightings and planetary symbols carved on the portal. It has served as a mosque since the Ottoman period, so you take your shoes off to see the vaulting and the blue-tiled eyvan.
season: Year-round; visit outside the five prayer times
tip: Look for the observation well in the middle of the floor and the tomb chamber on the left — the caretaker will explain the astronomy if you ask, and nobody volunteers it.
rev: Visitors find the observatory story fascinating and the building small but genuine; the drawbacks are that it functions as a working mosque with restricted hours, the interior is heavily replastered, and Kırşehir itself sees very few travellers.
onward: Ankara (ESB) airport 190 km or Kayseri (ASR) 150 km; the madrasa is on the main square in Kırşehir

name: Kaman-Kalehöyük
desc: A mound dug by Japanese archaeologists since 1986, its four superimposed levels running from the Early Bronze Age through Hittite and Phrygian to Ottoman — one of the cleanest stratigraphies in Anatolia. The site museum is buried into the hillside, and a Japanese garden with a teahouse sits next to it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the garden is at its best in late spring
tip: Come on a summer weekday during the dig season and you can watch the excavation from the viewing path, which is the only time the trenches are open.
rev: Praised for a genuinely good small museum and an unexpectedly serene Japanese garden; the caveats are that the mound itself is bare earth outside the dig season, opening hours are short, and it is well off any normal route.
onward: Ankara (ESB) airport, then 100 km southeast via Kaman; buses run Ankara–Kaman, then a taxi to Çağırkan

name: Lake Seyfe
desc: A shallow soda lake on the steppe east of Kırşehir, a Ramsar site where flamingos breed and thousands of waders stop on migration. There is no infrastructure beyond a track around the reedbeds and a hide — you park, walk to the shore, and listen to steppe larks with nobody else in sight.
season: Apr–May and Sep–Oct for migration; the lake can dry out entirely by late summer
tip: Approach from the Seyfe village side in the morning with the sun behind you — the western shore turns the birds into silhouettes all day.
rev: Birders value the flamingo colony and the absolute quiet, while every account notes falling water levels from irrigation, a lake that is sometimes just a salt crust in August, rough tracks and no facilities whatsoever.
onward: Ankara (ESB) or Kayseri (ASR) airport, then Kırşehir and 30 km east towards Mucur; car essential

name: Hirfanlı Reservoir
desc: A 263 km² reservoir on the Kızılırmak, built in 1959 and now the improbable inland sailing and fishing water of central Anatolia. Bare ochre hills drop straight into blue, small boat clubs operate from Kaman and Çiçekdağı, and pike-perch from the lake turns up on menus across the region.
season: May–Sep for swimming and boats; windy and bleak from November to March
tip: The Kırşehir side has the better shore access and the fish restaurants — the Ankara-side road is faster but has almost nowhere to stop at the water.
todo: Boat hire from the sailing club
rev: Locals treat it as their summer sea and the fish is genuinely good, but visitors report scrappy shorelines, litter at the popular access points, water levels that expose mudflats in dry years, and no organised facilities.
onward: Ankara (ESB) airport 150 km, then the Kırşehir road; shore access is easiest from Kaman by car
